A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same MAUBERT research. Text, figures, tables, equations and appendices support reliable comparison. Existing appendix content can be matched; v2 adds Appendices E and F.

before.justification: v1 reports original feature and phone recognition, ABX discrimination, speech-register adaptation and phonetic-inventory discovery results, including appendix Tables 7–8.

after.justification: v2 retains those original results and adds feature-level errors, spoken language modelling experiments and DiscoPhon evaluations in Figure 2 and Tables 9–13.

M1.justification: The FEAT/PHONE architectures, HuBERT adaptation procedure and four pseudo-label strategies are retained. v2 clarifies loss types and clustering operations and supplies a BLSTM rationale; these disclosures do not establish an altered MAUBERT algorithm. The added language model is used for downstream evaluation.

E1.justification: Appendix E adds language-model training on 6,000 hours of Libri-Light and English lexical, syntactic and semantic evaluations. Appendix F adds DiscoPhon phoneme-unit discovery evaluation across 12 languages, including Basque and Japanese beyond the original ten-language ABX suite. Original multilingual training and read/casual-speech coverage remain.

E2.justification: v2 removes WavLM-base+ and WavLM-large from both original ABX comparisons, Tables 3 and 4. The new spoken-LM comparison in Table 9 includes wav2vec 2.0, WavLM-base, DinoSR and SpidR alongside HuBERT-base; several scores are explicitly sourced from prior work. Extending retained baselines to DiscoPhon is not itself a comparator-set change.

E3.justification: New protocols include OPT-125M language-model training, vocabulary sizes of 100 and 256 with stated exceptions, and sWUGGY/sBLIMP/tSC evaluation. DiscoPhon adds many-to-one and one-to-one unit mappings, ground-truth-vocabulary fine-tuning, and PER, R-value, F1 and PNMI measurements. Existing ABX splits, training budgets and selection procedures are retained.

E4.justification: v2 adds per-feature error analysis in Figure 2 and reports that replacing the BLSTM with non-contextual networks degraded recognition and probing, although numerical ablation scores are absent. Appendices E–F further examine vocabulary/encoding choices and the consequences of enforcing phoneme-unit bijections, including deterioration in ABX performance.

E5.justification: Both versions report point estimates and averages across evaluation conditions. Neither supplies repeated-run counts, seed information, confidence intervals, statistical significance tests or comparable uncertainty estimates; the new experiments retain that reporting practice.

E6.justification: Retained entries in Tables 1, 3–4 and 7–8 are numerically unchanged, while WavLM result rows disappear. Figure 2 and Tables 9–13 add substantial results. For example, Table 10 reports fine-tuned MAUBERT-PHONE scores of 67.65 for sWUGGY-all, 58.83 for sBLIMP and 70.46 for tSC. Table 11 reports test PER of 32.51 for all-phones versus 32.70 for phone-frequency fine-tuning. These are newly reported evaluations, not improvements over matching v1 results.

T1.justification: The existing mathematical content, including the language up-sampling expression, is retained. The added appendices describe empirical metrics and mapping protocols without introducing new formal derivations, propositions or proofs.

C1.justification: The abstract, two stated contributions and conclusion retain the same claims about multilingual phonetic representations, limited-data adaptation and inventory discovery. The added introductory sentence reinforces existing low-resource motivation; the new appendix evidence does not redefine the headline contributions.

C2.justification: Appendix E explains that stronger ABX discrimination need not yield better zero-shot English language modelling and qualifies attribution because of English pretraining. Appendix F interprets phoneme-unit mapping difficulties and tradeoffs between assignment accuracy and representation quality. These substantially extend the interpretation, although some new ranking claims overstate their tables and the main ABX-only limitation remains unchanged.

D1.justification: v2 supplies a repository address where v1 only mentions released code, adds parameter counts, and clarifies losses, PER handling and clustering, including the sigmoid threshold of 0.5 and tie-breaking. Appendix E documents hardware, token budgets, context length, training steps, learning-rate schedule and checkpoint selection. Existing Table 6 hyperparameters are unchanged.

R1.justification: New citations support the added experiments, including Libri-Light, OPT, fairseq2, textually pretrained speech language models, DinoSR, SpidR and DiscoPhon. The main related-work organization and positioning relative to multilingual SSL and articulatory-feature research remain largely unchanged.

P1.justification: v2 locally expands the architecture rationale, rewrites clustering explanations, corrects cross-references and makes copyedits. Appendix D is renamed, and Appendices E–F are appended. The main section order and most existing prose remain intact, so the added scientific content does not amount to extensive narrative restructuring.

P2.justification: v2 adds the articulatory-feature radar chart and five result tables, expands Table 2 with parameter counts, and removes WavLM rows from Tables 3–4. Appendix tables are reflowed and relocated. The architecture diagram and original ABX plot remain, with the latter renumbered from Figure 2 to Figure 3.

improvement.justification: The new unit-discovery and language-modelling evaluations reduce reliance on ABX and reveal useful limits to zero-shot downstream utility; clearer implementation details also help. The net gain is limited by removed ABX comparators, the stale ABX-only limitation and new reporting errors. Appendix E calls Table 10's 76.48 a sBLIMP score, although it is in-vocabulary sWUGGY and sBLIMP is 58.83; Appendix F also misidentifies the best test PER in Table 11.
